g.text: The structure that must be fast and is safe to lose is not the structure that must be durable
A matchmaking ticket lives for seconds. A move is a permanent record. So the pool is the one piece of this design that is deliberately not in the schema.
written ONCE at start, updated ONCE at end
append-only, for the same reason a
A game has ONE row but potentially 80+ moves over its
life, each needing its own immutable record - one parent,
many children, and the children's write pattern (append
constantly, never update) is nothing like the parent's.
Keeping moves separate also means the in-memory
board_state a GameSession validates against and the
durable log serve genuinely different jobs: one is the
fast path for 'is this move legal right now', the other
is the permanent record AND the thing a restarting
instance replays to rebuild that fast path from scratch.
board_fen_after is denormalized onto EVERY move row, so reconstructing 'what did
the board look like at move 40' never requires replaying moves 1 through 39
first: a spectator jumping to a point in a game, or a post-game review tool,
The same 'freeze a value that is expensive to recompute' instinct as an
e-commerce total_amount or a conversation's last_message_at - a small amount of
storage now, against an expensive recomputation on every read later.
The other side: the matchmaking pool, which is not a database table at all
the rating-bucketed pool IN MEMORY (or Redis) - never on disk
A ticket's entire life is single-digit seconds - enqueue, get scanned by a
widening window, get matched or cancelled - so a durable round trip on every
tick's scan would be paying a durability cost for data that is cheap to lose AND
If a pool node crashes, the practical outcome is that a handful of waiting
players' clients notice their ticket vanished and re-issue the queue request: a
safe, cheap redo, nothing like losing a move or a rating update.
A blitz player must never be matched from a classical-only rating pool, which is why TIME CONTROL is the primary partition with
the rating-bucket structure nested inside it. And a single wildly popular time control - blitz, usually - can be split further
by a rating-band sub-hash if one partition's scan volume outgrows a node.
Indexes - each matching one query that actually runs
moves(game_id, ply_number) COMPOSITE: the single most common read in the system ('this game's moves, in order')
and simultaneously the idempotency backstop against a duplicate append for one ply
games(status, ended_at) the abandonment-timer sweep and any reconciliation job: 'games stuck active past their
expected end' - the same shape as the payments reconciliation index and the job
games(player_white_id, started_at) a player's own game history, most-recent-first: the query every profile page runs.
games(player_black_id, started_at) TWO indexes, because a player can be either colour and neither index covers the other.
players(rating) seeds the rating-bucketed pool at process start or after a full restart, AND serves
rating_history(player_id, applied_at) 'this player's rating over time' - the query a profile's rating graph runs
Consistency - including one place the in-memory copy IS the source of truth
games.status and the in-memory board_state during play
the IN-MEMORY BOARD is the strongly-consistent source of truth
a move applied at the owning Game Server instance is immediately the true current state, and any staleness here would be a
correctness bug in exactly the way a stale payment status would be.
strongly consistent relative to the in-memory apply
appended asynchronously but reliably, in the same logical step as it is applied to the board. Its OWN read pattern -
spectating, post-game review - tolerates replication lag: nobody's game-play correctness depends on how fresh a REPLICA of
the write must be immediately consistent
because it feeds that same player's NEXT matchmaking search, possibly seconds later - and a stale read here would bucket a
player into the wrong pool. Replicas are fine for profile browsing and leaderboard display: the same split between a write
path that must be current and a display path that can lag.
deliberately NOT durable across a crash
an explicit, accepted trade, not an oversight.
Sharding - and one place an arbitrary hash is the RIGHT answer rather than a cost
a game's full move history stays on ONE shard, so 'this
game's moves, in order' and the crash-recovery replay are
always single-shard operations - the same reasoning behind
players and rating_history -> by player_id hash
unlike a merchant-keyed payments ledger, a rating lookup is
always single-player and never needs colocating with
anything else - so an arbitrary, evenly-distributing hash is
the right choice here rather than a compromise.
the pool -> by time_control, then rating band
a correctness partition first (never match a blitz player
from a classical pool), a capacity partition second.
And the replica-versus-shard distinction once more: replicas solve read throughput for profile pages and rating-history graphs;
sharding solves the write volume and per-game locality that games and moves actually need. Reaching for one when the other is
the real bottleneck is the mistake to avoid.
Every choice traces back to a requirement
'never accept an illegal move, even from a modified client' -> the Game Server, never either client, runs isLegalMove
before anything is applied or persisted - which is also why
moves is a SERVER-WRITTEN append-only log rather than
something a client could post into directly
'a disconnected player can reconnect and resume' -> board_fen_after is persisted on EVERY move rather than only
at game end, so a restarting instance rebuilds board_state
from the last persisted row instead of losing the game
'a ticket lives for seconds, not the life of a game' -> the rating-bucketed pool is the one piece of this design
that deliberately is not in the schema at all
